what: Ionis Pharmaceuticals develops RNA-targeted medicines called antisense oligonucleotides, which switch off disease-causing proteins. It co-invented Spinraza for spinal muscular atrophy (sold by Biogen) and now sells its own drugs, Tryngolza for a rare lipid disorder and Dawnzera for hereditary angioedema, with more in late-stage trials.
customers: Patients with rare genetic and cardiovascular diseases, their specialists, and partner companies such as Biogen, AstraZeneca and Novartis that license its drugs.
money: Royalties on Spinraza and other partnered drugs, and milestone payments.
Sales of its own launched medicines.
moat: Three decades of expertise in antisense chemistry and a technology platform that has produced many approved drugs, with a large pipeline funded partly by partners.
risks: Losses are widening as it builds its own sales force: $547M over the last twelve months.
Spinraza royalties are declining as newer treatments compete.
Equity is small ($394M) after years of losses, though cash is ample.
Results of large heart-disease trials will decide much of the value.
opportunities: Cash of $1.9B and no reported debt fund the launches.
Its own launches move Ionis from royalties to product sales, with much higher margins.
Olezarsen, its triglyceride drug, could reach a large cardiovascular market if trials succeed.
Twenty-three analysts average a target near $68, more than double the price.
watch: Launch trajectories of its own drugs, and late-stage trial results in larger cardiovascular indications.
view: Ionis is at the most expensive stage of a biotech’s life: it is building its own commercial business after decades of licensing drugs to partners, so losses widened to $547 million over the last twelve months. The question is whether the launches can reach scale before the cash runs down.

The market values it at about $5 billion, roughly two and a half times its cash. Analysts’ average target is more than double the price, which shows how much the market discounts the pipeline. The decisive readouts are in large cardiovascular indications, where success would transform the revenue base and failure would leave a rare-disease company with a costly sales force.

This is a pipeline bet. The platform has a long record of producing approved drugs, which gives me more confidence than in most biotechs, but the outcome depends on a few trials. I would treat it as a high-risk position sized for disappointment, with genuine upside if the cardiovascular programmes work.
bull: Cardiovascular trials succeed, its own launches scale and Ionis becomes a profitable drug company.
bear: Launches are slow, trials disappoint and the cash runway forces dilution.
